steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a directionality-aware mixture model with parallel sampling for learning LPV dynamical system motion policies. Motivate DS-based policies, explain the limits of existing learning methods (NN-based, GMM and PC-GMM), and summarize our method and results.

steps.text:
- Motivation: robots in human workspaces and DS-based motion policies

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: robots in human workspaces and DS-based motion policies
  - safe integration in human workspaces -> adapt and replan as environments and constraints change
  - traditional path planning assumes known environment and dynamics; struggles with uncertainties, perturbations
  - Dynamical System (DS) motion policies: redundancy of solutions, infinite set of feasible solutions in one control law
  - stability conditions as constraints -> closed-form analytical solution to trajectory planning
- Goals and limits of existing approaches
  - stable, time-independent policies from limited demonstrations: i) state-space coverage, ii) minimal training data, iii) accuracy, iv) computational efficiency (online, incremental)
  - NN-based stable DS (normalizing flows, euclideanizing flows, contrastive learning): highly non-linear, but many trajectories, much computation
  - LPV-DS + GMM-based learning: achieves i-ii), but accuracy vs computational speed trade-off
- Problems of GMM and PC-GMM with trajectory data
  - GMM clusters sparse points, but no physically-meaningful representation; trajectories have directionality, GMM ignores it
  - fast Gibbs sampling inference, but misses motion/dynamic nature -> erroneous DS
  - Physically Consistent (PC)-GMM: state of the art, tailored to LPV-DS
  - distance-dependent Chinese Restaurant Process (DD-CRP) prior; pair-wise cosine similarity between every observation as directionality metric
  - better clustering and DS, but slow: similarity matrix, memory inefficiency, exponential increase in time wrt. data size
  - online learning hard: DD-CRP needs incremental, strictly sequential updates -> no parallel computation
- Our approach: DAMM and parallel MCMC sampling
  - Directionality-Aware Mixture Model (DAMM), inspired by clustering spherical data on Riemannian manifolds
  - proper Riemannian metric on directional data manifold -> physically-meaningful DS (Section III-A)
  - new parallel Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling scheme for DAMM, online performance (Section III-C)
- Evaluation and results
  - benchmarks: LASA datasets, PC-GMM dataset (2D and 3D real trajectories), vs PC-GMM and baselines (Section IV)
  - better DS across metrics, learning faster by order of magnitude
  - real robot experiments (Section IV-C): 500 observations in <500ms; first near real-time DS learning framework
  - schematic in Fig. 1; next section: LPV-DS, unit sphere geometry, Gibbs sampling

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
For robots to be safely integrated into human workspaces, they need to be able to adapt and replan when environments and constraints change. Traditional path planning approaches assume that the environment and the robot dynamics are known, and they have difficulties when there are uncertainties and perturbations during operation. Dynamical System (DS)-based motion policies, on the other hand, use the redundancy of solutions in dynamic environments: a single control law embeds an infinite set of feasible solutions, which overcomes environmental uncertainties and perturbations. Also, stability conditions can be added as constraints when learning a DS, which gives a closed-form analytical solution to trajectory planning.

We focus on learning stable, time-independent motion policies from limited demonstrations, with emphasis on i) state-space coverage, ii) minimal training data, iii) model accuracy, and iv) computational efficiency for online and incremental learning. Recent neural network (NN) based formulations for stable DS motion policies show promising results for encoding highly non-linear trajectories, for example with normalizing flows, euclideanizing flows or contrastive learning. But these NN-based methods need many trajectories and a lot of computation time to reach stable solutions. The seminal works on the Linear Parameter Varying Dynamical System (LPV-DS) formulation and its Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) based learning frameworks can achieve objectives i-ii), but it is a challenge for them to keep high reproduction accuracy without compromising computational speed.

GMM is useful for clustering sparse points, but it does not give a physically-meaningful representation of trajectory data. In trajectory planning/control applications, trajectories have an inherent directionality, but GMMs do not model directionality explicitly. Even though inference with standard Gibbs sampling is fast, a GMM has trouble capturing the intrinsic motion and dynamic nature of trajectory data, and this results in an erroneous DS. Physically Consistent (PC)-GMM was proposed to fix these issues; it is a state-of-the-art statistical model tailored to the LPV-DS framework. PC-GMM applies a distance-dependent Chinese Restaurant Process (DD-CRP) prior and integrates a distance metric of directionality by computing the pair-wise cosine similarity between every observation. Because it takes directionality into account as side-information, PC-GMM gives more informative clustering results and DS. However, inference in PC-GMM is slow, because the DD-CRP needs the similarity matrix to be computed, which is memory inefficient and makes the computation time increase exponentially wrt. the data size. Also, online learning with PC-GMM is hard, because inference with the DD-CRP prior needs incremental updates, and these updates are strictly sequential, so parallel computation is not possible.

To tackle these challenges we introduce the Directionality-Aware Mixture Model (DAMM). The DAMM formulation is inspired by related work on clustering spherical data on Riemannian manifolds, and it incorporates directional information by using a proper Riemannian metric on the directional data manifold. This way it captures the directionality within trajectories and produces physically-meaningful DS (Section III-A). We then introduce a new parallel Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling scheme tailored to DAMM, which can achieve online performance (Section III-C).

We evaluate our approach with extensive empirical validation, including benchmark comparisons against PC-GMM and baseline methods on the LASA datasets and the PC-GMM dataset (with 2D and 3D real trajectories) (Section IV). We show that the DAMM-based LPV-DS framework produces improved DS across various metrics, and that it learns faster than its predecessors by an order of magnitude. We also validate the approach in real robot experiments (Section IV-C), where a single batch trajectory of 500 observations can be learned in <500ms. To the best of our knowledge this makes our approach the first DS learning framework that can be estimated on a near real-time scale. Fig. 1 shows the schematic of DAMM-based LPV-DS in a typical robotic control workflow. In the next section we revisit the LPV-DS formulation and give a short overview of unit sphere geometry and Gibbs sampling.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Safe integration of robots into human workspaces requires the ability to adapt and replan in response to changing environments and constraints. Traditional path planning approaches, which assume a known environment and robot dynamics, face challenges when confronted with uncertainties and perturbations during operation [1,2,3]. In contrast, Dynamical System (DS)-based motion policies leverage the redundancy of solutions in dynamic environments, embedding an infinite set of feasible solutions in a single control law to overcome environmental uncertainties and perturbations [4]. Furthermore, stability conditions can be introduced as constraints when learning the DS, providing a closed-form analytical solution to trajectory planning [5,6].

Our focus is on learning stable, time-independent motion policies from limited demonstrations, emphasizing i) state-space coverage, ii) minimal training data, iii) model accuracy, and iv) computational efficiency for online and incremental learning. Recent neural network (NN) based formulations for stable DS motion policies show promising results in encoding highly non-linear trajectories, e.g. by adopting normalizing flows [7], euclideanizing flows [8] or contrastive learning [9]; however, such NN-based methods require many trajectories and substantial computation time to reach stable solutions. The seminal works on the Linear Parameter Varying Dynamical System (LPV-DS) formulation and its Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) based learning frameworks [6,10,4] can achieve objectives i-ii), but face the challenge of preserving high reproduction accuracy without compromising computational speed.

While GMM is useful for clustering sparse points, it fails to produce a physically-meaningful representation of trajectory data. In trajectory planning/control applications, trajectories have inherent directionality, which GMMs do not explicitly model. Despite its fast inference via standard Gibbs sampling, a GMM struggles to encapsulate the intrinsic motion and dynamic nature of trajectory data, resulting in an erroneous DS. To alleviate these issues, Physically Consistent (PC)-GMM was proposed [10], a state-of-the-art statistical model tailored to the LPV-DS framework. By applying a distance-dependent Chinese Restaurant Process (DD-CRP) prior [11], PC-GMM integrates a distance metric of directionality, computing the pair-wise cosine similarity between every observation. Using directionality as side-information, PC-GMM produces more informative clustering results and DS. However, PC-GMM suffers from slow inference because the DD-CRP requires computing the similarity matrix, leading to memory inefficiency and an exponential increase in computation time wrt. the data size. Moreover, online learning of PC-GMM is hard to achieve, since inference with the DD-CRP prior necessitates incremental updates [11] that are strictly sequential, ruling out parallel computation.

To tackle these challenges, we introduce the Directionality-Aware Mixture Model (DAMM). Inspired by related work on clustering spherical data on Riemannian manifolds [12], the DAMM formulation incorporates directional information using a proper Riemannian metric on the directional data manifold, inherently capturing the directionality within trajectories and producing physically-meaningful DS (Section III-A). We then introduce a new parallel Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling scheme tailored to the DAMM formulation that is capable of achieving online performance (Section III-C).

We evaluate our approach through extensive empirical validation, including benchmark comparisons on the LASA datasets [13] and the PC-GMM dataset [10] (including 2D and 3D real trajectories) against PC-GMM and baseline methods (Section IV). We demonstrate that the DAMM-based LPV-DS framework produces improved DS across various metrics, and learns faster than its predecessors by an order of magnitude. We further validate our approach in real robot experiments (Section IV-C), where a single batch trajectory of 500 observations can be learned in <500ms, making our approach, to the best of our knowledge, the first DS learning framework that can be estimated on a near real-time scale. The schematic of DAMM-based LPV-DS in a typical robotic control workflow is shown in Fig. 1. In the next section, we revisit the LPV-DS formulation and give a brief overview of unit sphere geometry and Gibbs sampling.
